hints: Focus on the type of structure and bonding in each chloride, as this controls how much energy is needed to melt it.
Spot that $\text{MgCl}_2$ is a giant ionic lattice with strong electrostatic attractions, so it will need far more heat than the other two.
Compare $\text{CCl}_4$ and $\text{PCl}_5$ as simple molecular substances, then decide which has stronger London forces from its larger size and greater number of electrons.
walkthrough:
**Classify each chloride by structure**

Start by asking: ionic lattice or simple molecules? $\text{MgCl}_2$ is a metal plus non-metal, so it forms a giant ionic lattice. Both $\text{CCl}_4$ and $\text{PCl}_5$ are non-metal chlorides, so they exist as simple discrete molecules.

Structure types:
$$\text{MgCl}_2 \text{ : giant ionic} \quad \text{CCl}_4, \text{PCl}_5 \text{ : simple molecular}$$

**Place the ionic compound highest**

Melting an ionic lattice means breaking many strong ionic bonds in all directions between $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ and $\text{Cl}^-$ ions. This needs a lot of thermal energy.

Result:
$$\text{melting point of } \text{MgCl}_2 >> \text{melting point of molecular chlorides}$$

**Order the two molecular chlorides**

Melting a molecular solid only overcomes weak London (induced dipole) forces between molecules, not the strong covalent bonds inside. Larger molecules with more electrons have stronger London forces.

$\text{PCl}_5$ has a larger $M_r$ and more electrons than $\text{CCl}_4$, so its intermolecular forces are stronger and it melts higher than $\text{CCl}_4$.

Final order lowest to highest:
$$\text{CCl}_4 < \text{PCl}_5 < \text{MgCl}_2$$

options.A: Correct. $\text{CCl}_4$ is lowest because it is small and molecular with only weak London forces. $\text{PCl}_5$ is next because it is also molecular but larger with stronger London forces. $\text{MgCl}_2$ is highest because of its giant ionic lattice with strong electrostatic attraction.
options.B: Incorrect. This puts $\text{MgCl}_2$ lowest, which reverses the key idea. Giant ionic lattices have very high melting points, not low ones, because strong ionic bonds must be broken.
options.C: Incorrect. This puts both $\text{MgCl}_2$ lowest and $\text{CCl}_4$ highest. $\text{CCl}_4$ cannot be highest as a small non-polar molecule with only weak intermolecular forces.
options.D: Incorrect. This correctly puts $\text{MgCl}_2$ highest but swaps the two molecular chlorides. $\text{PCl}_5$ is larger than $\text{CCl}_4$ so it has stronger London forces and a higher melting point, not lower.
